strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: controllable, compositional generation of 3D anatomical segmentations for biophysical simulation, without requiring retraining for new constraint combinations.

The core idea of guiding an unconditional diffusion model with differentiable, geometrically-normalized moment losses (mass, centroid, scale-normalized covariance) applied per-component is simple, clean, and well-motivated, and enables disentangled control (Algorithm 1, Sec 4).

Extensive experimental evaluation, including conditional fidelity, morphological distribution similarity (pair plots, Frechet distance), point-cloud metrics (MMD/COV/1-NNA), a disentanglement ablation (Table 1), and a compositional-generation comparison against a strong dropout-based conditional baseline (Table 2), which the proposed method generally outperforms, especially with few constrained components.

Reasonably comprehensive set of baselines for comparison (explicit/implicit conditioning with ANG, cross-attention with CFG), which strengthens the claim that inference-time guidance outperforms training-time conditioning for flexible constraint composition.

A compelling downstream demonstration linking geometric guidance to biomechanical simulation (RV inpainting and FEM pressurization), illustrating practical utility for form-function studies, plus reasonably thorough appendix with implementation details supporting reproducibility.
Clear writing and figures that effectively illustrate the qualitative behavior of the method (disentangled control, compositionality).
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to a single anatomical domain (cardiac CT segmentations from TotalSegmentator, one dataset, one VAE/LDM backbone), raising questions about generality to other anatomies or modalities; no experiments on a second dataset/organ system to support claims of broad applicability.

The geometric guidance is limited to fairly coarse, low-order moments (mass/volume, centroid, second-order covariance ellipsoid); complex or non-ellipsoidal shape variation (e.g., branching vasculature, local curvature) is only qualitatively shown (Fig. 12) without quantitative assessment of fidelity for such structures.

Quantitative gains over the strongest baseline are sometimes marginal (e.g., Table 2 at higher component counts, geometric guidance and implicit conditioning are comparable), and the paper's own text acknowledges this ("performance of implicit conditioning is similar to that of geometric guidance" at higher component counts), somewhat weakening the generality of the compositionality claim.

Hyperparameters (loss weights λ) are tuned experimentally per loss term (Sec 8.4.1) rather than through a principled or automatic procedure, and the paper notes this as a limitation but does not explore sensitivity or robustness of results to these weights beyond a single configuration.

No comparison against more recent/stronger inference-time guidance baselines beyond self-guidance-style loss guidance (e.g., other attribute/text-based guidance schemes cited in Sec 2), and no user study or clinical validation of anatomical plausibility beyond automated morphological/point-cloud metrics.

The biomechanical simulation demonstration (Sec 5.8) is a single toy case study (one patient, RV enlargement/shrinkage) without quantitative validation against ground truth or broader cohort-level analysis, limiting the strength of claims about enabling counterfactual biophysical studies.

Some potential instability issues (unstable gradients for near-empty segmentations, need for noise regularization in mass denominator) are mentioned as limitations but not deeply analyzed empirically (e.g., failure rate, frequency of topologically incorrect outputs).

strengths: Proposes a training-free, inference-time guidance framework for controlling unconditional diffusion models of 3D anatomy using differentiable geometric moment losses (mass/size, centroid/position, and scale-normalized covariance/shape), avoiding the need to retrain conditional models for every new constraint.
Demonstrates clear disentangled control over size, shape, and position both quantitatively (Table 1 ablation, ordering effects of each individual loss) and qualitatively (Figures 7-9).

Shows strong compositional generation capability: guidance can be applied to an arbitrary and varying number of anatomical components without retraining, and clearly outperforms an implicit-conditioning baseline with dropout when few components are constrained (Table 2, Figure 11).

Fairly comprehensive experimental comparison against multiple reasonable baselines (explicit concatenation, implicit concatenation/heatmap conditioning, cross-attention) combined with standard guidance mechanisms (CFG, adaptive null guidance), using both conditional-fidelity metrics and generative-quality metrics (Fréchet distance, precision/recall, MMD/COV/1-NNA).

Includes a compelling downstream application to biomechanical simulation (RV pressurization FEM) illustrating practical utility for counterfactual/'digital sibling' anatomy generation, which strengthens the significance of the contribution beyond pure generative modeling metrics.
Reasonably detailed appendix covering dataset curation, hyperparameters, guidance/baseline implementation, and evaluation protocol, aiding reproducibility.
Honest discussion of limitations (need for manual weight tuning, gradient instability for near-empty masks, topological artifacts).
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to a single anatomical domain and dataset (cardiac structures derived from TotalSegmentator CT, 596 cases after filtering); it is unclear how well the moment-based ellipsoidal guidance generalizes to other organs/modalities or to anatomies with more complex, non-ellipsoidal topology (e.g., highly branching vasculature, thin/curved structures) beyond the limited qualitative examples in Figure 12.

The geometric guidance loss weights (λ0, λ1, λ2) are tuned experimentally per loss type rather than derived principledly or learned; this manual tuning burden is acknowledged as a limitation but not deeply analyzed (e.g., sensitivity across datasets/components is not shown).

No runtime/computation-cost comparison between guidance-based sampling (which requires backpropagating through the VAE decoder and moment computation at every denoising step) and the conditionally trained baselines, which is an important practical consideration for adoption of a training-free method.

"Anatomical realism" is assessed purely via morphometric and point-cloud statistical metrics (FD, precision/recall, MMD/COV/1-NNA) without any clinical/expert qualitative validation or downstream task validation beyond the single illustrative biomechanical case study, so claims of clinical plausibility remain only weakly supported.

Topological correctness (disconnected structures, spurious components) is explicitly acknowledged as unresolved and left to future work, which could limit reliability for the stated simulation use-case.

Second-order moments (covariance) only capture coarse ellipsoidal shape approximations; fine-grained or highly non-convex shape control is not really achievable, limiting the expressiveness of the "shape" guidance term relative to more flexible shape representations.

The comparison baselines are conditionally-trained models that must be retrained for each new constraint set, which is somewhat structurally disadvantaged relative to a training-free guidance method by design; a more apples-to-apples comparison (e.g., against other training-free guidance techniques for anatomical geometry, if any exist, or stronger conditional baselines with more expressive conditioning) would strengthen the significance of the reported gains.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: bridges the gap between rigid conditional training and flexible geometric control for anatomical generation, targeting real biophysical simulation use cases (virtual cohorts, digital twins).

Technically clean formulation: differentiable geometric moment functions (zeroth/first/second-order voxel moments for mass, centroid, scale-normalized covariance) enable interpretable, energy-based guidance of an unconditional latent diffusion model without retraining.

Broad and thorough experimental protocol: multiple quantitative metrics (conditional fidelity L1, morphological precision/recall/FID-like distances, pointcloud MMD/coverage/1-NNA), ablations for disentanglement (size/position/shape independence), multi-part compositionality, dataset-scaling analysis, alternative second-moment decompositions (extent/stretch/orientation), and autoencoder reconstruction bounds.

Demonstrates generality across four distinct anatomical systems (cardiac, aorta, spine, knee) and shows a concrete downstream application via FEM biventricular pressurization simulation on edited anatomy, illustrating practical utility beyond image synthesis.

Extensive, detailed appendix with hyperparameters, dataset curation, and additional analyses supports reproducibility and transparency about design choices and limitations (e.g., Betti-number topological errors, editing scale-factor breakdown).
weaknesses: Inconsistent baseline reporting: three conditional baselines (explicit concatenation, implicit concatenation, cross-attention) are introduced, but the key compositionality comparison (Table 1) only reports 'Implicit' vs 'Ours', leaving open whether the strongest possible baseline was used for that comparison.

No wall-clock/computational cost analysis: the method requires backpropagating a geometric loss through the VAE decoder and diffusion denoiser at every sampling step, which likely incurs substantial overhead relative to conditional (single-pass) baselines, but this tradeoff is never quantified.

Quantitative evaluation is concentrated almost entirely on the cardiac dataset; the aorta, spine, and knee datasets (Section 5.8/Figure 12) are only assessed qualitatively, so claims of 'generality over anatomical systems' are not rigorously substantiated.

Guided samples show increased topological (Betti) errors relative to unconditional/reconstructed baselines in several structures (Table 8), indicating the geometric guidance can occasionally degrade anatomical plausibility, a concern only partially addressed as a stated limitation rather than mitigated.

The ellipsoidal/second-moment representation is inherently coarse (captures only up to second-order shape statistics) and cannot express localized or sub-structure geometric features, limiting applicability to more nuanced anatomical control tasks.

Guidance weights require manual per-loss tuning (Table 4), and while the paper claims good transfer across anatomical systems, this is only lightly validated and could be a barrier to practical deployment on novel structures.

Limited statistical rigor: most figures show line/scatter plots without confidence intervals or significance testing across the ~100-200 sample evaluations, making it hard to assess robustness of reported trends.
